asBirthCard.p: This one comes from the birthdate alone, so it says nothing about your Sun or Moon or anything else in the chart. Add every digit of the date, keep going until the total is 22 or under, and yours landed on twelve, either straight away or by way of 39, 48 or 57. Twelve is a one and a two sitting side by side, and if you add those you get three, which is The Empress, the card of things growing. That's worth keeping in mind with a card that looks this still. It sits between Justice, who has just weighed something up, and Death, where something actually ends. So The Hanged Man is the stretch in between, after the verdict and before the change, when you're hanging there waiting to find out what you think. The card belongs to Neptune, the planet of water and fog and things you can't quite pin down, and it carries that nature with it. It tends to blur edges, between plans, between roles, and between where you stop and someone else starts.

You're usually the last one to decide. At a work meeting everyone's got a view by the second slide and you're still turning it over, and then two days later you send an email that changes the whole plan, because you came at it from the other end. A group chat about where to go for dinner can sit unanswered on your side for hours, and it isn't that you don't care, you genuinely can't tell yet. People find that maddening and occasionally very useful. On a free Saturday you can lie on the couch half the afternoon without a phone in your hand and call it a good day. You also tend to put things down for a while, a book, a friendship, a half-finished degree, and pick them up years later as if hardly any time had passed.

Most people are terrible at waiting. They refresh the inbox, ring the agent again, invent a story so there's something to do. You're oddly good at it, and that turns out to be useful to other people. A friend is waiting to hear about the job interview, or the visa, or whether the house sale went through, and you're the one they want around, because you don't fill the gap with guesses. You'll make tea and talk about something else and let the not-knowing just sit there in the room with you both. The same thing helps in a negotiation or a family argument. You can leave a silence alone long enough that the other person finally says what they meant. Friends tend to ring you in those weeks, sometimes before they've told anyone else.

The less obvious trouble is that waiting can become a way of choosing without having to say so. You don't break up, you just stop suggesting plans until the other person ends it. You don't turn down the promotion, you let the application deadline slide past. The lease renews itself because you never rang the agent. Then if it goes badly, well, it wasn't really your decision, and that's a very comfortable place to stand. Neptune makes it worse, because the card's planet is good at fog. Ask you straight out what you want and you'll say you don't mind, and sometimes that's true, and sometimes you just don't want to be the one who wanted it. The people close to you can usually tell which it is before you can.

When something goes wrong you tend to go still first. Bad news on a Tuesday and you might not tell anyone until the weekend, and in between you carry on with the dishes and the emails as though you're fine, while most of you has gone somewhere else. A week on you're usually sleeping a lot or very little, and you've started giving things away, taking on extra at work, covering a friend's shifts, lending money you haven't really got, as if being useful to somebody will make the bad thing make sense. The people around you find it hard because there's nothing to grab hold of. You're not angry and you're not crying. You're just a bit absent. What helps is one person you tell early, and something physical with a start and an end, a swim or a long walk to a particular place, so the waiting has a shape.

In love you're often the one who sees someone upside down, which is to say you see the version of them nobody else has noticed yet. The shy colleague who turns out to be very funny. The person everyone else wrote off after the divorce. That's lovely, and it's how a lot of twelves end up in long, good relationships that surprised their friends. The catch is that you can fall for the version you've spotted and keep waiting for it to arrive, and waiting is the one thing you'll do for far too long. You'll also soak up a partner's moods until you can't tell whose bad day it is. Every so often it's worth asking yourself whether you're with the person in front of you or the one you're hoping for, and saying so out loud if it's the second.

Work with waiting built into it suits you better than you'd expect. Research, editing, anything with long lead times, gardening, night shifts, conservation, the kind of planning job where a file sits for a month and then needs someone who still remembers it. You're good at the second look, the one nobody budgeted for, and a lot of twelves end up as the person who spots what's wrong with the plan everyone else has signed off. The strain comes in workplaces that reward whoever talks first, because you'll often have the better idea and say it on Thursday. You also tend to give a job more than it gives back, staying late for a manager who wouldn't do the same for you. Write down what you've agreed to do each week, and treat anything outside that list as a favour you're choosing to do.

At twenty a twelve often feels behind. Friends have picked a course, a city, a partner, and you're still working out what you think, and people say 'you'll figure it out' in a tone you don't love. There's often a stretch in the twenties where life just stalls for a year or two, a family member who needs looking after, a gap after study, a job that holds you in place, and it feels like wasted time while it's happening. By the mid-thirties a lot of twelves can look back and see that the stuck year was where the real decision got made. The fifties tend to bring a looser grip on how things turn out, and a better sense of when to wait and when to get down off the tree and walk. That second part usually takes the longest to learn.

When you notice you're waiting on something, a reply, a decision, someone else's move, write it on a sticky note with a date beside it, the date by which you'll act whether or not anything has changed. Stick it inside a kitchen cupboard door where you'll see it most mornings. When the date comes, do the thing, even if it's only sending one message. Keep the old notes in a drawer. After a year or so you'll be able to look through them and see which of the waits were worth it.
